analysis.one_liner: Lets local governments cap basic cable TV rates where the cable company faces no real competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee; no committee vote, no floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1984 Cable Act left cable rates almost entirely unregulated, on the theory that competition would keep prices down. This bill would have let local franchising authorities regulate basic cable rates and equipment charges whenever a cable system lacked effective competition. It set a detailed test for what counts as competition — including a rule that a company cannot count a rival it owns or partly controls — and gave cable operators a court challenge if regulators found they had no competition. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers in communities served by a single cable operator, who would gain protection from rate increases if their local franchising authority found the system lacked effective competition and chose to regulate rates.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a local franchising authority to regulate the rates for basic cable service and for installing or renting receiving equipment whenever it finds the cable system is not subject to effective competition.

Defines effective competition with a numerical test: a community counts as competitive only if a rival multichannel video provider is available to at least 67 percent of multichannel households and rival services collectively exceed 30 percent of those households.
Bars a cable system from counting a competitor that is owned or controlled by the same company or its affiliates, closing the loophole where a cable operator cites its own subsidiary as competition.

Presumes a system faces competition only if fewer than 30 percent of households that could get cable actually subscribe, and requires regulators to revisit their findings periodically as market conditions change.
Gives cable operators judicial review of adverse findings, with a court able to set aside a finding only if it lacks substantial evidence.

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, who would lose pricing power in markets where they face no real competitor; if regulation depressed rates, operators and their investors would bear reduced revenue, and some of the burden of compliance and litigation would fall back on ratepayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill's competition test is narrow: a community is presumed competitive only under strict thresholds, so regulators could impose rate caps in markets where some genuine alternatives exist, discouraging cable systems from expanding or upgrading.

Rate regulation would be run by local franchising authorities, which vary widely in expertise and capacity, and the bill leaves each authority to design its own regulatory method, inviting inconsistent treatment of similar systems.
Operators facing rate regulation could litigate, and the bill's own review process — while requiring substantial evidence to overturn a finding — would add delay and cost to regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For subscribers in towns with one cable operator and no cable-length rival, the bill offered a direct check on prices after Congress had stripped rate regulation in 1984. The costs are real but modest by design: regulation only triggers where the bill's own test finds no effective competition, operators keep a court challenge, and a system with low penetration or genuine rivals is presumed competitive. The main design weakness is handing rate-setting to local authorities with uneven capacity, and the narrow thresholds could cap rates in some markets that were becoming genuinely competitive.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 1989 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up; no vote ever happened, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Cable Television Subscriber Protection Act of 1989 on April 18, 1989, joined by Senator Joseph Lieberman.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The action record shows no further action — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired with the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991.
Only two senators cosponsored the bill, both Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators came out ahead: with the bill never reaching a vote, they kept the unregulated rate structure of the 1984 Cable Act and avoided local rate caps in the monopoly markets the bill targeted.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let local authorities regulate basic cable rates where cable systems lack effective competition.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Lieberman.'

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 18, 1989 and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the action history.

against.name: Cable television industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed the return of cable rate regulation and lobbied Congress against it during the late 1980s cable rate debates.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled Commerce Committee never acted, so the bill's fate was decided inside a Democratic-run committee without a recorded party split.

industries.note: The bill would have allowed local rate caps on basic cable service and equipment charges wherever a cable system lacked effective competition, directly limiting operators' pricing power. Cable operators' interest in stopping the bill ran against subscribers, who bore the unregulated monopoly rates the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Competing multichannel video providers (satellite and wireless cable services)
industries.note: The bill defines these services as potential competitors that can establish effective competition and shield cable rates from regulation, but only if they are independent of the cable system. Independent rivals would benefit from the clear test; rivals affiliated with cable operators would be disqualified from counting.
